learningObjective: Understand why a custom operator must provide a meta / FakeTensor implementation to be compatible with torch.compile.
stem: A user registers a custom CUDA kernel via `torch.library` and calls it from a `torch.compile`d function. Which statement most accurately explains what the 'meta' (aka FakeTensor) implementation is for?

options.text: The Meta implementation lets Dynamo / AOTAutograd trace the custom op without actually executing it: it propagates shape, dtype, and device without touching real data, enabling FakeTensor propagation and downstream analysis (shape guards, fusion boundaries).

The Meta implementation is required by Inductor to convert the CUDA kernel into Triton code; without it, Inductor recompiles the CUDA implementation into a Triton equivalent from LLVM IR at trace time. In this reading, the Meta implementation is required by Inductor to convert the CUDA kernel into a Triton equivalent; without it, Inductor recompiles the CUDA implementation into a Triton kernel from LLVM IR at trace time using a source-to-source translator.

The Meta implementation only matters for TorchScript export; torch.compile does not use it and instead runs the CUDA kernel eagerly during tracing. Under this framing, the Meta implementation matters only for TorchScript export; torch.compile does not consult it during tracing and instead runs the actual CUDA kernel eagerly to observe the concrete output shape and dtype for each traced call.

Meta implementations are deprecated in favor of DispatchKey::CompositeExplicitAutograd; providing one causes torch.compile to skip the CUDA implementation entirely at runtime. In this account, Meta implementations are deprecated in favor of `DispatchKey::CompositeExplicitAutograd`; providing one now causes torch.compile to skip the CUDA implementation entirely at runtime, silently falling back to the composite ATen decomposition.

explanation: During torch.compile tracing, ops are executed on FakeTensors that model shape / dtype / device without holding real data. To trace a custom op, PyTorch calls its 'meta' implementation to propagate output shape/dtype/device symbolically. Without a meta implementation the tracer either graph-breaks or errors. The meta impl does not turn CUDA kernels into Triton and is not a TorchScript-only artifact.

optionExplanations.A: Correct: standard reason for providing a meta impl.
optionExplanations.B: Wrong: meta impl does not drive Triton codegen.
optionExplanations.C: Wrong: torch.compile relies on meta impl.
optionExplanations.D: Wrong: meta impls remain the standard mechanism for custom op tracing.

assumptions: The custom op is called only through torch.ops.mylib.my_gemm (not via Python-level dispatch that would bypass the meta impl).
nonImplications: Does not imply the meta impl must be perfectly accurate for every dim; obvious symbolic propagation suffices.
Does not imply Inductor fuses the custom op with surrounding pointwise ops; opaque custom ops typically form fusion boundaries.
